answer: The passage wasn't included with your question, so this answer draws on general knowledge of graph-based spectral methods (e.g., Laplacian Eigenmaps, diffusion maps, and related approaches), not on the specific text. Such methods scale mainly by (1) building a sparse k-nearest-neighbour graph, which costs roughly O(n log n) with tree-based search and keeps storage at O(nk); (2) working with sparse graph matrices (Laplacian or affinity) instead of dense n×n matrices; (3) computing only a few extreme eigenvectors with iterative solvers (Lanczos/Arnoldi, LOBPCG, or power-type methods), which cost roughly matrix-vector products rather than a full eigendecomposition; and (4) optionally using Nyström or landmark extensions, random projections, or polynomial/Chebyshev filters to approximate the embedding. By contrast, PCA needs the eigendecomposition or SVD of a d×d covariance matrix or a dense data matrix. Its cost is O(min(nd², n²d)), though truncated or randomized SVD can reduce this. Classical IsoMap is the least scalable: it computes all-pairs geodesic distances (roughly O(n² log n) via Dijkstra), stores a dense n×n doubly centred kernel, and performs a dense eigendecomposition costing about O(n³). Landmark IsoMap mitigates this by computing geodesics only to a subset of landmarks and triangulating the rest.
